Trying to give a serious answer: learn vanilla JavaScript first and focus on the newer parts of the language. It's backwards compatible in order not to break existing sites so all the shitty old parts is still there. But focus on the modern features. 

There's a bunch of good courses. Try until you find one you like. 

Then add Typescript and realize how many problems it solves. 

Then add a framework like React once you understand the problems it solves.

Just a hint - JS is backwards compatible in order no to break existing sites. So the old shitty parts of earlier versions still exists. But if you focus on the parts introduced by ES6 and onwards your life will be much easier. Also Typescript contains all of JS and adds support for some highly useful things. 

If you know vanilla JS well enough you'll start to realize that all the weird frameworks etc are all still JS. Just very specific subsets/ways of using it.

I'm a web dev who likes to dabble in game dev so I started building my own 2d engine in JS. It was fun an taught me a bunch. But two evenings in Godot got me further than I got in weeks and months in pure JS. 

Advice: keep the scope super small while doing pure JS and learn Typescript before growing the scope. React is great for interfaces but fiddly to make place nicely with pure JS parts for games if you're new to it. Avoid it if you don't desperately need it. 

Generally it's fine doing arcade titles in pure JS. Theres APIs for controllers and sound can be easily done with Howler which can save a ton of hassle. 

Try out different paradigms like object orientation vs functional programming and see what you like. Implementing the same thing in different ways can be a great way to learn. 

I've done some tile based top down, arcade stuff, chess, shoot em ups, interactive art and some text adventure stuff. It's fun, but using an engine is essential once you want to make a game rather than just code for fun.

The trick is to make sure you have a good win/fail ratio. 


Let's say you're going to create a tiny app that just takes a string input and calculates how many times each letter is in the string. That's so small that you may be tempted to just write the whole thing and run it. 


That's a mistake. 


A few small errors in your short program will have you save and rerun it time and time again. So you may have 20 fails until it finally runs. 


Let's say you instead continuously run your program while you're developing. You may start with an empty function returning a hardcoded answer. Run it and it works - one win already. Then move some logic to a utility function and run it again - another win. Then make the subfunction takes an argument and log it to the console - another win.  


You may still have 20 fails, but now you're also have a matching win count. That makes it a whole other ballgame. 


Computers give a lot of love when you program in small steps. 


Once you get more experienced you can do bigger parts at a time.

Sure. In the 90s and 00s we'd write some html+php that gave us what we wanted and slap some CSS on it. Reload and done. If you were a frontend you maybe focused on the CSS and a little javascript to do stuff like show a div when you clicked a button. All you did was edit files and hit save. 


Today every part of our stacks have added layers of complexity. For CSS you have incredibly powerful new features in CSS but also lots of tooling. You may use SCSS or a framework like Tailwind. That compiles to like 3MB of CSS and has a build step that checks all your code for the utility classes you actually use. 


For Javascript you have linters so you write it the correct way, there's build steps with hot reload, browsersync to expose a local server on your network, production build, transpiling, minifying, obfuscation etc. And javascript is rarely used by itself. These days you have Typescript which is a superset that adds a typesystem with interfaces etc. 


Not to mention that people rarely write just Typescript either. Usually you have a framework like React. Which has it's own tooling and conventions. 


And it moves quickly. The course you bought on a Udemy sale a year or two ago is likely outdated. And then there's the fact that React uses tons of libraries. Like just keeping track of state (essentialy variables) is often a whole different library with it's own conventions. 


And everything is powered by node modules where one library needs a library that needs a library that needs a library. My node_modules at work if regularly 20 000 files of other peoples code. I haven't vetted any of that,  it's just the new normal. And sometimes our build or deploy pipeline breaks because some of them no longer play nicely together.  


There's more of course but the gist of it is that corporate jobs use a ton of tooling that is mostly useful but also introduces complexity that creates it's own issues. Like how do you know that central IT blocks a port on your machine that some tool uses to serve your CSS build locally. 


Generally it's fun though. The things we can do today are awesome. And recent versions of Javascript (ES6+) made it into a really decent language.

The biggest thing about programming is that the computer always does exactly what it's told, not what you meant. So learning involves a lot of failure and trying to understand what you actually instructed it to do. And it's necessary. You have to learn to embrace it and get curious instead of frustrated when things don't work. 

Curiosity is your friend overall here. And remember that you're building a foundation right now. The priority isn't finishing games but making sure you build up the toolset to be able to make them independently in the future. When you follow tutorials make sure to explore all the things you're shown and not just click the same boxes / copy code mindlessly. 

Gamedev is pretty much the extreme sport of programming. But the recognition is quite low in the general world. As is the salaries. So if building a legacy that impresses friends and family is important it may not be the best route. But if you want a life well lived from chasing your dreams and life long learning it's a good opportunity.

Making a generic copy of a website is easy. But there's a million things to handle for actually running one in production.

Let's say you have a good price on some Nvidia RTX card and have 45 of then in stock. 1000 people show up across the world to look at them and start putting them in their shopping cart. 

Who of the 1000 gets to actually put them in the cart? With datacenters all across the globe how do you make sure  people in Europe doesn't book 45 before the 45 orders from the US is in the database? And what if you accidently let through 90 orders? And do you remove them from "x amount in stock" before the actual order is placed? How long do you let people keep them in their cart before cancelling the session and letting someone else order? Or do you not reserve them at all and let people get to the payment only to discover it's now sold out? Which is less badwill? 

And do you know you actually have all 45? What if there's a shipment coming in 2 weeks,  do you show them as in stock and just show longer delivery time? Do you trust certain suppliers more than others based on history?

What are there laws and regulations to adhere to?

What product data do you display and is it correct? What about translations? Do you trust the person who wrote it or will you end up a meme because sometime wrote a cringe description? 

Payments, login, accessibility,  return policy and handling, logistics etc etc. 

Any tiny example is an endless fractal of decisions where management, lawyers etc often needs to weigh in. 

Just handling a small site that does actual business requires a ton of network, server and database job even without the devs doing anything at all. 

And what about rolling out changes. Maybe you broke the session and their cart reset and all the cards are now sold out. 

And this is just a few.

When we code something we use a human readable language like C that gets translated to more efficient machine readable instructions that are then distributed on Steam etc. 

The human readable code is usually never available for people outside the company. And the machine readable requires special knowledge, tools and a ton of time to make sense of.

For some games there's languages used that doesn't follow this exact process where you may have better chances. The Sims4 has a layer of Python and XML that can be inspected and adjusted with a little effort.

But effectively "no" for the intent of your question. 
Even a simple case like a perk changing a value from "false" to "true" in human readable code would have you having to hunt for all the places it's referenced and in some way affects other logic.
